headline: Bay water pushes into the 70s, and the fluke and bass follow the current out the inlet
subhead: New moon springs build toward a big weekend — Shinnecock Inlet's outgoing tide is where I'm putting my nights.
body_markdown:
Last week the bay finally caught up to summer. Shinnecock Bay's been sitting in the mid-to-upper 70s, and that kind of warmth does something predictable if you've fished this water long enough — it pushes the fluke right out of the flats and into anything with current and depth. I watched it happen over four nights on the water: the drift off Tiana that was holding decent fish two weeks ago went quiet, and the channel edges by the Canal and the inlet mouth started producing instead. Warm, slack bay water doesn't hold fluke long in July — they want moving water and a temperature break, and right now that break is sitting right at the inlet where upwelled ocean water, running close to 71 degrees, is meeting the warmer stuff sliding out on the tide. That seam is the whole story this week.

We're heading into new moon, peaking around July 11-13, and that means the tide swings are building — bigger floods, harder outgoing, more water moving through the inlet in less time. For a night guy like me, that's the green light. Bigger springs mean the outgoing rips harder off the jetties, bait gets pulled out with real force, and the stripers stack up in the eddies waiting for it. This is the first true nighttime window we've had since the June full moon set up, and I don't take that lightly. If the wind cooperates — and right now it looks manageable out of the south-southwest, nothing that's going to blow the inlet into chop — Friday through Monday night should be the best stretch we get this month.

Striped bass have been the most consistent thing I can point to, and they're doing it exactly where they're supposed to: the outgoing tide at Shinnecock Inlet, working the north jetty rocks and the back side structure toward the Coast Guard station. Eels have been the closer after dark — a 7-inch live eel, no weight, drifted right along the rock face on the last three hours of the outgoing. Guys throwing bunker-spook style pencil poppers at the top of the tide have picked off a few too, but the eel bite in the dark hours has been the more dependable pattern. Fish have run 24 to 34 inches mostly, with a couple of better ones pushing 20 pounds coming off the deeper pocket where the inlet channel bends toward the ocean side. Nothing blitz-style, but a hookup every 20 minutes on a good tide isn't a bad night by any measure.

Fluke have shifted, like I said, and the inlet mouth and the deeper channel water running out toward the ocean are where I'd put my rod right now instead of the mid-bay drifts that were producing back in June. Four-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow on the last two hours of the outgoing in 12 to 18 feet, have been the ticket. A few boats working the deeper hole just inside the inlet on the ocean side have found keeper-class fish to 22 inches mixed with a lot of short fish, so it's not a fish-a-drift bite — you're covering water and culling through some throwbacks to find the better ones. Chartreuse bucktails tipped with squid strips have worked when the current's really ripping and you need something with more flash to get down.

Ponquogue Bridge has been holding weakfish, though I want to be straight about this one — it's a bite, not a blitz. Working bucktails tipped with a strip of squid or a Fishbites strip along the pilings after dark, on the last of the outgoing when the current sweeps bait past the structure, has produced fish in the 2 to 4 pound range with a scattered 5-pounder mixed in. It's a slow, patient bite, best fished from a boat anchored just up-current of the pilings so your presentation swings naturally into the shadow line. If you're not getting bit within the first 30 minutes of a tide stage, it's usually not going to happen — move rather than grind it out.

Porgies are steady but unspectacular around the inlet rocks and the deeper bay structure near the Canal mouth, clam on a standard rig doing the job for anyone who wants a mixed bag or a chance at a bonus blackfish holdover. Bluefish have been running through the inlet in short pushes, mostly smaller choppers chasing bait on the outgoing — good fun on light spinning gear with a metal lure if you catch the timing right, but they're not staying put long.

Looking ahead, the new moon springs building into the weekend are what I'd plan around. If the current at the inlet really loads up like I expect Friday through Sunday night, that's when I'd fish the eel bite hardest on the outgoing — the harder the current, the more the bass commit to the eddies along the jetty. If that doesn't produce, the backup is the fluke drift right at the inlet mouth where the temperature break is holding — that pattern should stay reliable as long as the bay keeps running warm and the ocean keeps feeding cooler water in on the tide. Worth checking the Canal connection into the Peconic side too if the bay stays sluggish; that link has bailed out plenty of slow weeks for me before.
